## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mahāassārohajātaka* (Ja 302) is a story in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional narrative framework, the Buddha delivered the tale while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Elder Ānanda, teaching that in former times the wise also recognized that one good turn deserves another [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. The story opens in the commentary with the verse incipit *Adeyyesu dadaṃ dānaṃ* [Fausböll 1883].
In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is the King of Bārāṇasī who encounters a villager after suffering a defeat in battle; disguised as a great horseman, he is treated with hospitality and promises a future reward if the villager visits the city [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. In the concluding identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the border villager is revealed to have been Ānanda in a past existence, while the king was the Bodhisatta himself [Fausböll 1883]. The verses emphasize themes of gratitude, the rewards of beneficent action, and loyalty among friends [Anandajoti 2010].
Curated parallels in external Buddhist traditions are not reported by SuttaCentral [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus registers no cross-language matches above the score threshold, but identifies Pali-internal text sharing across segments §1.1–4.4 with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (volume 3) [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral lists four translations of the text in four languages [SuttaCentral].
